fixes.answer: I consider it one of the most serious challenges facing humanity, if not the most serious. The scientific consensus is overwhelming, and we are already witnessing its effects through more frequent extreme weather, rising sea levels and disrupted ecosystems. Its potential to cause widespread displacement, food insecurity and conflict is genuinely alarming. So while some still [[downplay]] it, I believe it is an [[existential]] threat that demands urgent, [[decisive]] action.

This is a matter of both responsibility and capability. I believe richer, industrialised nations bear a greater responsibility, as they have contributed the most historical emissions and have the financial resources to lead. It seems only fair for them to do more, including helping poorer nations. However, developing countries, some of which are now major emitters, must also participate. So the burden should be shared [[equitably]], with the wealthy [[shouldering]] a [[proportionate]] load.

The effects on people are wide-ranging and increasingly severe. More intense heatwaves, floods and storms directly threaten lives and homes. Changing weather patterns disrupt agriculture, [[jeopardising]] food security and livelihoods. Rising seas endanger coastal communities, potentially creating large numbers of [[climate refugees]]. There are also serious health impacts. So climate change is not merely an environmental issue; it is a profound [[humanitarian]] one that threatens the stability of entire societies.
fixes.why: 'threatens', 'stability', 'societies' are plain; marked 'jeopardising', 'climate refugees', 'humanitarian'; softened the 'millions' figure

fixes.answer: The difficulty lies in competing national interests. Countries worry that ambitious climate action will harm their own economies and competitiveness, so many are reluctant to act unless others do too. There are also disputes over who is most responsible and who should bear the costs. Powerful industries [[lobby against]] change as well. So despite the shared threat, short-term [[self-interest]] and a lack of trust often [[hinder]] the global cooperation required.

I believe we still can, but the window is closing rapidly and it will require unprecedented effort. The technology and knowledge to transition to a clean economy largely exist; what is often lacking is the [[political will]] and global cooperation. If we act decisively now, we can still limit the damage, though some impacts are already [[inevitable]]. So I remain hopeful, but only if we treat it with the urgency it truly [[warrants]].

The most effective solutions involve rapidly [[transitioning away from]] fossil fuels towards renewable energy like solar and wind. Improving energy efficiency and protecting and restoring forests, which absorb carbon, are also crucial. Government policy is key, from [[carbon pricing]] to investment in green technology. Individual lifestyle changes help too. Essentially, it requires a coordinated [[overhaul]] of our energy, transport and consumption systems on a global scale.
fixes.why: 'global' and 'scale' are plain; marked 'transitioning away from' and 'carbon pricing'

fixes.answer: I partly agree but find the statement [[disempowering]]. It is true that systemic change by governments and industry is far more impactful than individual action alone, so no one should feel the entire burden rests on them. However, I disagree that individuals are powerless. Collectively, our consumer choices, our voices and, above all, our votes exert real pressure that drives the bigger changes. So individual action is not [[futile]]; it is part of a larger [[momentum]].
